strengths: The paper studies a practically relevant phenomenon: SAM can improve test accuracy while increasing membership leakage, challenging the use of generalization performance as a privacy proxy.

The empirical evaluation covers five datasets, multiple architectures, and both direct and modern shadow-model attacks. Some increases are meaningful: CIFAR-100 online LiRA TPR at 0.1% FPR rises from 27.0% to 31.0%, alongside improved test accuracy.
The memorization and influence analyses offer useful exploratory evidence, while ASAM/GSAM comparisons broaden the observation beyond standard SAM.
weaknesses: The central theoretical model is not derived from SAM. Section 5 substitutes minimum-G-norm interpolation with G = I + eta Sigma, using population covariance. For linear squared loss, all exact interpolators have identical empirical SAM sharpness; using the empirical covariance in G also leaves the minimum-norm interpolator unchanged. Thus, the variance result concerns an imposed surrogate geometry and does not establish the claimed inherent effect of SAM.

The likelihood-ratio guarantees have substantive gaps. Lemma 11 requires member variance to exceed non-member variance, which is not established by Assumption 1 or required in Corollary 5. The latter is false as stated: with member variance 1, reducing non-member variance from 4 to 2 decreases optimal LR advantage from approximately 0.323 to 0.166. Theorem 3 also combines an unconditional Gaussian member distribution with a non-member distribution conditioned on the fitted model, without reconciling these probability spaces.

The proposed influence-entropy metric and subgroup comparison need stronger foundations. Influence scores can be negative, and Equation 5 is undefined when all scores vanish; Appendix H.2 assigns these cases maximal typicality by convention. It also reports different bucket memberships for SGD and SAM. Without an explicitly matched comparison on identical test examples, Figure 4 cannot cleanly attribute accuracy differences to atypical-sample generalization.

The claimed causal mechanism exceeds the empirical evidence. Memorization-score ranges, selected influential pairs, and a few visual examples do not establish that SAM selectively learns rare subpatterns rather than other sample-specific information. The paper does not directly quantify the proposed non-member variance reduction or connect it to individual membership leakage. Controlled subgroup interventions and measurements of the relevant output distributions are needed.

Statistical uncertainty and reproducibility remain insufficient. Although shadow-attack results average ten splits, no confidence intervals or variability estimates accompany the reported differences. The comparison of newly computed SAM memorization scores with public SGD scores does not adequately document matched training configurations or estimation budgets, and several optimizer and shadow-training details remain incomplete.
